transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hello, Doctor. I'm Tom. Well, I'm here because I'm having a real problem with my eating. It's... what scares me most is that once I start eating, I just can't seem to stop. It feels like my hands just keep reaching for more and more food, even while I'm sitting there telling myself, 'Tom, stop this right now.' I just completely lose control over it, and I don't know what to do anymore.
When you're eating and can't stop, what feelings or emotions are you experiencing at that moment? For example, are you feeling anxious, stressed, sad, or numb?

Well, to be honest with you, Doctor... I'm not really sure. I don't think I feel anxious or sad, or anything specific like that. I haven't really noticed any particular emotion while it's happening. 

It's just... I'm just eating. I don't really know how to describe what I'm feeling, to be honest, other than just knowing I can't stop myself. I just haven't really paid attention to my emotions in that exact moment.

After these episodes where you can't stop eating, do you do anything to try to counteract or undo what you've eaten? For example, do you make yourself vomit, use laxatives, exercise excessively, or restrict your eating afterward?

Yes, I do. After I eat like that, I get... well, I get really worried about all that food just sitting inside me. So, sometimes I'll go into the bathroom and make myself throw it back up. And... I've also taken laxatives a few times, just to try and get it out of my system faster. I just feel like I have to do something to get rid of it.

When you have these episodes where you eat a lot and can't stop, do you feel like you've lost control over your eating during those moments, or does it feel more intentional—like you're choosing to eat that much?

Well, like I was saying earlier, it definitely doesn't feel intentional. I absolutely feel like I lose control. It's... it's like I was telling you, the scariest part is that once I start, my hands just keep grabbing more food. I'll be sitting right there, clear as day in my head, thinking, 'Tom, you need to stop this right now,' but I just can't. My body just keeps going even though my mind is telling it to quit. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm choosing it at all.
How often do these episodes happen where you lose control and eat a lot? For example, do they occur several times a week, once a week, or less frequently?

Well, I actually keep food logs, so I have a pretty clear record of it. Looking at those... for many months now, it's been happening nearly every week. 

There's almost always at least one afternoon a week where I just eat completely out of control like that. And then, afterward, I try to make up for it. Like I mentioned before, I'll use laxatives or make myself throw up, but sometimes I'll also just fast and not eat anything, or I'll really push myself hard with a lot of walking and doing heavy chores around the house to try and work it off. So, yeah, it's at least once a week.

When you use laxatives, make yourself throw up, or exercise after eating, what is your main concern or worry that's driving you to do those things? Are you worried about gaining weight or how your body looks, or is it something else?

Well, it's definitely about my weight. My doctor keeps telling me I'm too thin, but... if I step on the scale and it's up even half a pound, I just feel panicky. I get this overwhelming sense of shame, like I've completely let myself go. That's when I feel like I just have to fix it right away, and that's why I do those things. I just can't stand the thought of gaining weight.

When you have these episodes of eating that you can't control, would you say you're eating an unusually large amount of food—significantly more than most people would eat in a similar situation—or is it more of a normal amount that just feels out of control to you?

It's definitely a lot more than most people would eat. It's... it's a huge amount. On those afternoons when I'm alone at the house, I can just keep going. I'll go through a whole loaf of bread, a jar of peanut butter, a box of cookies, whatever leftovers are in the fridge, and then a tub of ice cream... all in one sitting. And I do all that before I even really look up or realize what I've done. So, yes, it's an unusually large amount of food.

You mentioned your doctor says you're too thin, but you panic about small weight gains. When you look at yourself in the mirror or think about your body, how do you feel about how you look? Do you see yourself as overweight, or do you worry about becoming overweight even though you know you're actually thin?

Well, I don't really see myself as overweight right now, exactly. I know what the doctor says, and I know I'm on the thinner side. But... when I look in the mirror, all I can focus on is the fear of getting fat. 

It's just this constant worry that if I'm not careful, if I don't catch every little pound, it's all going to spiral out of control. I just can't stand the idea of my body changing or getting bigger. So, even though I know I'm thin, the fear of becoming overweight is always there, hanging over me.

You mentioned these episodes happen at least once a week, and you use laxatives, make yourself throw up, fast, or exercise heavily afterward. Over the past three months specifically, would you say that on most weeks when you have a binge episode, you're also doing one of these compensatory behaviors—or does that only happen sometimes?

Yes, it happens every week. I actually keep food logs, and if you look at them, they show that for many months now, nearly every single week has had at least one of those afternoons. I'll eat completely out of control, and then right after, I try to make up for it. I'll either make myself throw up, take laxatives, fast the next day, or just push myself really hard with walking and doing heavy chores around the house. So, yes, it's pretty much a weekly thing, and it has been for a while.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets full criteria for Binge Eating Disorder with purging subtype (F50.81). Key diagnostic features confirmed: (1) Recurrent binge episodes characterized by loss of control and consumption of objectively large quantities of food (entire loaf of bread, jar of peanut butter, box of cookies, ice cream in single sittings); (2) Frequency of at least once weekly for many months, meeting the minimum threshold of once per week for at least 3 months; (3) Regular compensatory purging behaviors (self-induced vomiting, laxative use) and restrictive behaviors (fasting, excessive exercise) occurring after nearly every binge episode; (4) Marked distress about binge eating and weight/shape concerns; (5) Fear of weight gain despite being objectively thin, with panic at minor weight fluctuations; (6) Clear loss of control during episodes with inability to stop despite conscious effort. The purging/compensatory behaviors and the focus on weight/shape concerns distinguish this from non-purging binge eating disorder.
